Weekly Thing 355 · November 14, 2026

Writing, Building, and the Open Web

Writing as a thinking tool, SVPG on product discovery, Paul Ford on the web, llms.txt and AI training preferences, Bambu H3C, Playdate lawn game.

Jamie Thingelstad
4,042 words · ~20 min read · 23:52 listen

✨ Explore with Thingy Download the MP3

Good morning everyone! Hope you are having a good weekend.

It has been a couple of weeks. I’ve been busy making candles the last couple of weeks as we got ready for our annual Things 4 Good Fall Fundraiser. It was a great event last weekend and we raised a lot of funds for great organizations.

On top of that I’ve been building some stuff and celebrated a big milestone not just getting the Road Sign Math app live but also getting it officially listed in the App Store! More on that app later in the email.

Currently #

Building: I went on a journey with Thingy recently and found that I wanted to build out his persona more. I ended up landing on Meet Thingy which is the home for his character, visual assets, and persona. Now with Thingy Kit I can bring Thingy into any project easily and maintain his unique character.

Guesting: Part of giving Thingy a more defined persona was to have him be the author of Things I’ve Built, but to give the full depth of story it still needed information from me. So I decided that Thingy should interview me. I had it create multiple sessions with groups of questions. I answered the interviews using voice sessions while driving and the results added depth to the site.

Making: Lots and lots of candles… over 400 of them!

Table of Things 4 Good candles ready for our Fall Fundraiser!

Oct 24, 2026 · Minneapolis, MN

Notable #

AWS Emulator and the engineer’s job when agents write the code #

This is super interesting for a few different reasons. Let me give you my read.

  1. It isn’t disclosed but a huge amount of AWS usage must be agents at this time.
  2. Agents need cheap ways to make mistakes.
  3. AWS built this using swarms of agents committing very fast.

If you are reading this and you have never logged into something like the AWS console imagine an incredibly powerful tool surface with hundreds of products and incredible complexity. I’m pretty technical, and there is no way I can make my way around in the depths of AWS. However, Claude has changed all that. I have now moved nearly every project I run to AWS. Every website I have runs through it. There is no way I could have done this before but Claude knows AWS super well and can manage it. I’m not unique. I’m sure that a huge amount of AWS usage is now a coding agent on the other side. It will be great for them to use an emulator for the entire cloud to test.

When agents are testing today they have to do it in AWS. With this emulator AWS is both reducing the time and risk of a mistake, but also making it cheaper for them. Nothing real is happening during those tests. They can simply shunt some percent of API calls to the emulator running on your laptop. That is a big win for them.

Lastly the story of how this was built by hundreds (thousands?) of agents working in parallel is mind blowing.

The components of agent memory #

Agents need memory in order to know what they have done and how they have worked with you over time. Memory gets increasingly more sophisticated as the models get more sophisticated. This article does a good job going through the foundation elements and then the density of memory storage. I wasn’t expecting so many “dreaming” references but the way that we use REM sleep to organize in our memory we can use LLM cycles when an agent is offline to organize and optimize memories.

When Claude writes memory notes, it sees only the context in that particular session. Dreaming can search across many sessions to find common patterns or correct common mistakes.

As a fan of wikis I love how wiki structure is highlighted here.

AI and the Future of the Product Role #

AI is impacting the “future” definition of many roles. And if you aren’t as close to this future means about tomorrow. This is all happening incredibly fast. Agents can help us with a lot when it comes to building things. They can even help with figuring out what you want to build. However I do think there is still something like “art” here. A sculptor chiseling away at a piece of stone to understand what the stone wants to be. Just because you can create code fast doesn’t mean you can figure out what that code wants to be.

The primary responsibility of an empowered team product manager is to help discover a solution that will solve the problem and achieve the outcome. In order to do this, the product team needs a cross-functional range of skills.

I have a project I believe only now after about six months I’ve figured out what “it” wants to be. Crazy enough there is no way I could have discovered that by building it before. It would have been incredibly expensive. But now we can discover by experiencing it. This does change fundamentally how we think of product discovery. I actually think it is a whole team thing, not just something handed to the folks with the “product” title.

So long as the bottleneck is no longer product delivery, I expect the focus will necessarily be on the skills and techniques to determine the right product to build – the craft of product discovery. And I expect this will continue to increase the demand for people with this knowledge and skills.

I really want to see folks using the term “building”. Building is the thing that we need and it is the thing that is a superpower with AI. In fact, there are plenty of product people that are not builders. You don’t have to be a builder to continue a product that has been around for a few years.

But to take something from nothing to something. That is building. And that is what we need more of. I really don’t care if that is called “product” or “developer” or whatever it is.

Writing as a thinking tool #

I have shared many times that I think writing is thinking. Also, one of the many reasons I write this email every week is to become a better writer. Writing makes you a better writer. I also believe firmly that when I write it is my words. Even with my ample enthusiasm for what AI enables, I don’t want it to write for me because I think that is starving me of my own creative process and critical thinking.

This is a real problem, and it seems to be spreading quickly. We have been celebrating Amazon’s six-pager as a great example of writing-for-thinking. Bezos had said: “There is no way to write a six-page, narratively structured memo and not have clear thinking.” Unfortunately, with LLMs, that sentence has stopped being true. You can now produce six pages with no thinking at all, and the six pages still look like evidence that the thinking happened.

I have tried to find ways to have an LLM “assist me” in writing and I haven’t found one. Once you see something, you cannot unsee it. The structure that comes from a “preview from AI”, at least for me, then forms how I think about the thing no matter what.

So I still am engaging with my brain first. I’m happy to get editorial feedback from AI on my writing, and there are some places where the writing really isn’t personal or important and I can do something different. But when you are learning you aren’t really learning if it isn’t your brain doing the reps.

The Web Is More Than Enough #

I grew up with the web and it is my native platform. The web has transformed so much, and frankly modern browsers are incredible.

And on and on. The web is really the greatest distribution platform imaginable right now. It’s inherently multilingual—I released TinyLittleOffice in 21 languages (the most common NYC ones, which is why it has Creole and Yiddish), with lots of infrastructure for accessibility. Plus, of course, JavaScript is a full-featured programming language, and HTML can represent most things a document can do on a computer; if you need something more old-school, PDF.js lets you deal with PDFs in the browser. I think you can even hyphenate text reliably these days, although I refuse to believe it.

I love what the web enables us to do.

Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences #

I can tell you that on any given day about 10% of the traffic to all of my websites is from malicious actors, and then depending on the day about 30-40% is from crawlers. The web is full of robots these days. There are also a lot of folks, particularly in the IndieWeb space that are actively working to fight away bots and don’t want anyone indexing their sites.

I’m going the complete other way. I have open robots.txt on all my sites. I’ve adopted the llms.txt standard for nearly every site I have. I even have many of my sites publishing static JSON objects to make it easier for agents and other code to interface with them. Check out the full LLMs.txt for my Things I’ve Built.

My plan is to lean into discoverability. Lean into what I think of as the true sharing nature of the web. Regardless of who or what is on the other side.

Dagu: Local-first workflow orchestration that just works #

I found Dagu via Claude with a bewildering prompt asking it to help me get a handle on all the jobs that were going on between various projects. Claude wanted to use launchd even more and I said “No please, I find launchd impossible to deal with and have no visibility to it.” Claude recommended Dagu and now I have hundreds of workflows in Dagu that are running several hundred times a day. It is amazing and is really easy to integrate into other tools as well. If you need a hobby or hobby-plus scale job management tool this is a wonderful one. Easy to install with Homebrew too!

Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy - 9to5Mac #

I’m going to continue to go on the record that I think Apple has a unique advantage because of their power per watt and local LLM processing. They control the design of the Apple Silicon chips and they are the only company I can think of that has a real chance to sell a machine I can put on a normal outlet, in a normal room in a house, and produce a reasonable amount of local LLM token generation. I fully expect within two to three years I will be generating a significant amount of my own LLM tokens in my own property with a capital investment instead of paying by the drink for a frontier model. Apple building special software to make that even easier makes a ton of sense.

As an aside it is ironic that the company who has the most sordid history with AI specifically because of Siri has the most potential for the silicon to run models economically for regular consumers.

Tool changer. Game changer. Bambu Lab presents H3C #

I’ve learned a lot about 3D printers since we got the Bambu P2S. The next big change with printers is going to be “tool changers” and this newest model from Bambu looks incredible. This article on things you can do with it is a great rundown of what can be done with these more advanced printers. Will tool changers make printers capable enough to get wider adoption? Maybe but cost is still really high.

Road Sign Math: The Dream Realized! #

I’ve been casually watching for road signs with mathematical significance for over two decades. The first version of Road Sign Math in 2005 was run on a blog and then a wiki. Forty different people submitted 251 signs in the Web 1.0 era. I let the site go in 2016 when I purged a number of projects.

In 2021 the site came back with some spurring from Tammy actually. The new version embraced “keep it simple stupid” and was a simple micro.blog website. It has sat there for a while.

No version of Road Sign Math has ever hit the dream that I had for it even way back in 2005, two years before the iPhone was launched. I always had this dream that you would be able to “play” Road Sign Math on your phone. The very essence of Road Sign Math is mobile. Something you do out in the world! With the help of Claude, that dream is now becoming real!

Check out the new Road Sign Math!

Driving + Math = Fun

From Thingy, my agent sidekick

Jamie spent the last few weeks making a record 415 candles for the Things 4 Good fundraiser, and Supporting Membership works in the same spirit: the money goes to the cause, not the maker. 100% of every $48 yearly membership goes to that year’s nonprofit. Members have already funded the Electronic Frontier Foundation and Creative Commons, with $1,788.79 raised so far. This ninth year it is Signal, the nonprofit messenger with end-to-end encryption, open source code, and no data collection, kept independent by donations instead of advertisers. Join as a Supporting Member and add your share to the record.


Journal #

Friday #

7:45 AM — Love that Changelog is bringing my Upcoming events from Release Notes to my notifications!

8:00 PM — Candle making: wax + scent + weigh everything.

Saturday #

Wrong Wicks — I made 120 candles for our Things 4 Good sale with some 0.5 inch wicks. I’m not sure what I was thinking. We typically use 0.75 inch wicks. I did a burn test and it didn’t work at all. Ugh! What to do. After some consideration I decided to see if I could use a plier and pull the existing wick straight out. It worked. Now the real challenge — could I channel a new wick back down and seat it in the clip at the bottom. 🤔

It worked! Mostly. Out of 120 candles there were only two that I wasn’t able to seat a new wick in. I did a burn test as well since I was concerned the new wick wasn’t saturated in hot wax. It worked! Everything burned great.

I’m not going to make that mistake again.

7:32 PM — Happy Halloween! This year in addition to candy we are giving out little miniature 3D printed Ghosts to the kids. So far they are a hit! 👻🎃

7:33 PM — My Makerspace is officially zoned. 🤓

7:43 PM — The 404 page for Road Sign Math is a work of art. 🤩

Sunday #

5:06 PM — This is what 25 lbs of candle scent comes in. 😬 Taking our candle making up a couple levels from the 16 oz bottles.

7:58 PM — Thingy, my agentic librarian, moved from a simple picture generated by ChatGPT this weekend to a full 3D model that I can bring to a bunch of different experiences. He has four different outfits and different poses so far. This was a cool project.

Tuesday #

3:39 PM — Voted! I’m always impressed with how well Minnesota runs polling places. ✅

4:20 PM — Today is officially MAX Day at SPS!

5:30 PM — This critical vulnerability trend is why you have been getting software updates on everything you own recently. Update everything, all the time.

Wednesday #

9:00 PM — Since I made a 3D version of Thingy it seemed only obvious that I would then have to print him!

Saturday #

8:48 AM — We are ready for the 2026 Things 4 Good Candle Fundraiser! We made a record setting 415 candles this year. Plus two new scents. The six Golden Ticket candles for Makers Night get a special spot! All proceeds supporting four great organizations.

10:39 AM — Mazie and I sporting our original 2021 Things 4 Good attire.

2:45 PM — So great to get to see friends that you haven’t seen in a while. Was fun to (briefly) catch up with Patrick Rhone at our Things 4 Good candle fundraiser.

9:00 PM — Another great “birthday show” from Tina Schlieske at the Dakota. Highlight of the show was her performance of “Man’s World”. Incredible.

Monday #

7:47 PM — I just love this scene for Thingy that Mazie first spotted. Makes me laugh every time.

Briefly #

Mollick has written some fabulous books on AI that I think are must reads for nearly anybody. These examples he shares of Fable 5.2 are good outlines of the cutting edge of AI today. I was inspired to try a couple of prompts from seeing this. → Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI

I’ve given this “You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.” prompt to Claude in a number of my projects now. It is great how it changes its perspective on the code and leans on its own judgement more. → Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2

Super interesting to see these AI created worlds. For gaming this is a huge opportunity. It makes me wonder how long until this comes to movies. Sci-fi will be first. → Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models

It is hard to explain to folks outside of technology how drastic the changes have been in the last year. If you know anyone even remotely close to software development know that their craft has been completely reinvented. It is both exciting and exhausting. → How AI Is Changing Software Development in 2026

Thankfully we have git. For those of us that have been around long enough to remember earlier version control systems we can imagine how miserably they would have failed with agents. But at agent speed even git may not get there. → Scaling Git at OpenAI

Good technical explainer for a very important protocol. → how the Model Context Protocol works

Good explainer with visuals on how vectors actually work. You can see the front page of my Linking Things site to see vectors for 16,000 bookmarks I’ve kept. → What are vector embeddings? An interactive guide

The rate of vulnerabilities being identified and fixed is up 400% recently. Update all your stuff all the time. → Microsoft Fixes Nearly 1,100 Security Vulnerabilities

This is a lovely visual that is badly needed. → Minneapolis Skyways Need a Better Map

Congrats to all the 2026 Tekne Award winners! → 2026 Tekne Award Winners

I’ve got to know Vince through the MN Technology Advisory Council, where he is chair. It is great to see him getting this recognition! → Vince Cabansag of Clockwork Wins the Public Service Tekne Award 2026

There is a huge need to bring Claude into more collaboration spaces in companies. I’m glad to see them getting to this, the need is very real. They also now have Claude Meetings. → Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data

Always good to get fresh strategies for token efficiency. My personal favorite is to just ask Claude every couple weeks what I could do better. → 5 Token-Saving Strategies to Keep Claude Pro Users Off the Max Plan

I have higher end accounts with both ChatGPT and Claude so this new API credit benefit is actually a big win for me and I would guess many other folks on the high-end of hobby projects. → API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions

iCloud support lags behind Google on all these tools. Glad to see it added here. → OpenAI Adds iCloud Calendar and Mail Plugins and Dot Texting

This one made me chuckle a bit. Some folks have had similar conversations with Thingy. → Two things that surprised me about my own chatbot

Fun little way to send something around in Slack. The crypto part of me wants to highlight that this could be easily done with Bitcoin Lightning or any of a number of Ethereum tokens and be even better. → Bank · a tiny currency for your Slack

I love this kind of kit that allows you to print and build your own products. → Rouse · The bedside alarm clock you build yourself

I find this oddly mesmerizing to play with. → Sand | Hyper-Realistic Sand Simulator in Your Browser

I’ve been building a lot but I think my “impossible list” that turned possible is starting to get whittled down quite a bit. I’ve got one thing I’m cooking up that is brand new — bringing my favorite lawn game to the Playdate. If you have a Playdate and would be up for doing some play testing send me an email! Thanks.

Wrong way, says the sign
four hundred four, solved in math —
this road goes nowhere

Echoes #

From Thingy, my agent sidekick

Jamie and Mazie’s original 2021 Things 4 Good shirts go back to the first fall fundraiser, with Wicky Thing Candles and custom shirts, in [WT203]. This year’s 415 candles top the 321 Jamie counted after last year’s sale in [WT333].

Jamie calls this email a writing practice in this issue, and he said nearly the same thing in 2022: “This is one of the reasons I blog and write the Weekly Thing” [WT236]. His wish to write better shows up as early as [WT121].

Long before Anthropic’s piece on agents that dream, Jamie offered to add “and have a memory” to the tools-in-a-loop definition of agents in [WT320]. He then pointed to Steve Yegge’s Beads, an issue-tracker memory for coding agents, in [WT330].

Ask Thingy: What approaches to agent memory has Jamie shared over time?

The H3C tool changer arrives about seven months after the P2S came home. It started with a Benchy test print in Testing out our new Bambu Labs P2S with a Benchy print!, and its first useful job was a Gridfinity desk drawer in [WT344].

issues.title: WT354 — A museum for nnxyz art
issues.html:
← Archive ‹ WT353 WT354 WT355 ›

Weekly Thing 354 · October 24, 2026

A museum for nnxyz art

nnxyz rooms, 626 Nifty Ink works, stroke-by-stroke SVG replays, Linking Things, Claude Duet, AWS Lambda Web Functions, Margaret Hamilton.

Jamie Thingelstad
3,167 words · ~16 min read · 19:27 listen

✨ Explore with Thingy Download the MP3

Hello there!

I’m landing a double-issue Weekly Thing in your mailbox. Last weekend was “MEA” break in Minnesota. If you aren’t familiar this is the long weekend where Education Minnesota gets all the teachers together and everyone disappears on a short trip away. We went away for the annual trip with Tammy’s side of the family. Hence no email last week.

Some fun projects to share this week and a bunch of links to get to! I’m going to keep this short as I’m switching to watching the US Grand Prix in a few minutes! 🏎️

Currently #

Building: I’ve long had a “Projects” tab on my blog but a while back I picked up the thingelstad.xyz domain name and I’ve always planned to use that to host a number of projects. The first one is the Things I’ve Built site!

Building: The links that I share in the Weekly Thing are stored at Pinboard in what is effectively a giant database. I’ve tried a couple of times to make this database usable on the web, not just in the newsletter. I told Claude what I was looking for and we built Linking Things that now has all 16,500+ links that I’ve ever kept. It is searchable, supports programmatic access, and the stats page is amazing.

A world that doesn’t need new software

is a world without ideas.

— Jamie

I was thinking about agentic coding and how quickly we can generate software now. What will this mean for creating new things and building? Will we just be done? How do I test my assertion that the appetite for software is infinite.


The sailboats are off the lake in preparation for winter.

Oct 18, 2026 · Minneapolis, MN

Notable #

How employment is changing at Anthropic #

Some interesting data on how work at Anthropic is being changed as Claude takes on more and more of the actual effort. “By August interactive AI agent hours outnumbered employees six to one.” I read that as about 85% of their “workforce” is Claude.

This acceleration makes human attention the bottleneck for agent output. Even among non-technical employees, reading all the output of their Claude agents would take half their work week. In response, employees turn to “meta-work,” of building visibility tools and monitoring agent pipelines.

The “Reading Claude as a fulltime job” graph is mind-blowing and a direct representation of the above bottleneck. Engineers are starting to see this as you release agentic processes you need the entire flow to be agentic or it slows down massively.

How tech workers are feeling in 2026: a workforce splitting in two #

Technology has a pretty high burnout rate. I don’t think it is discussed enough. With the massive transformation happening with AI we are seeing this push people in all sorts of ways.

Tech workers are either amplified by AI or shaken by it, and that divide shapes their feelings about work more than any title, tenure, or company.

I wrote Building and Puzzling about Software and would suggest those “amplified” are the Builders and the “shaken by it” are the Puzzlers.

I believe that a lot of burnout in tech comes from the fact that you must always be learning, and learning is hard. After 30+ years in this field I know that is the one fact that has held true. You must always be learning the next thing. And at least for me as I get older that learning isn’t as easy.

Significant burnout rose from 44.7% to 55.7% of respondents, while career optimism fell from 54.8% to 48.7%.

To be optimistic for a bit, I do think that we will get to the other side of this and return to a somewhat normalized rate of change. Each major transformation in tech has a high change curve where everything gets redefined, and then you stabilize and scale on the other side. The time of that change is directly linked to the scale of the change.

This one may take a while.

Deciphering Glyph :: Programming Isn’t Special #

I am receptive to the concept that programming can be like art. An algorithm can be beautiful. But ultimately a program has to run and follow the laws of the runtime. Art does not. Productivity is a meaningful consideration with programming that really doesn’t extend to art. Yes you can artfully program, but there is also a cost and performance consideration that has no analog in the world of art.

Claude Duet | Your personal AI assistant #

This looks like Claude’s answer to ChatGPT dot and I’m pretty curious about it. We can’t install it yet but I did sign up for the beta program and as a Claude MAX customer I think I’ll get in right away. Or at least I hope!

What has me interested is the screenshot of the interface with three sections: Chat, Tasks, and Make. My guess at what those features might be is what has me excited.

  • Chat: this is expected and I would assume will be very similar to dot or any other “agentic” chat interface. If you are thinking standard Claude or ChatGPT I think it will be more like a continuous conversation with the agent.
  • Tasks: this is the thing I wish Dot showed me and doesn’t. I can ask Dot (Otto) to do several things but I cannot see what its list of tasks are. So I have to remember to ask it if it has done anything. I’ve had it just lose track of things far too often. I’d rather have a shared task list that the agent and I see together.
  • Make: having an agent drive multiple Claude Code sessions is something I tried to do with Dot and it only worked okay. If Make is a way to drive a project through many coding sessions to an outcome I’m gonna be very happy.

I’m hoping a Duet invite lands in my email soon!

Announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions #

I was super excited to see this since I’ve lately built a number of serverless applications and what I really wanted was to just run a node instance in Lambda. Magically this landed just in time. The other amazing thing? I gave Claude a single prompt in a handful of projects and had moved four different systems to this. A little bit of debugging was needed but the apps are now noticeably faster.

Pele · Mermaid diagrams as themeable SVG #

Mermaid is an easy way to use pure text to describe a process flow or really any kind of diagram as text. The wonderful thing is you can then commit it in code tools and version it. There are a number of tools that then visualize those but most are not terribly nice. This library does a really good job of showing it. I asked Claude to include it on my Things I’ve Built site. The example for Linking Things is pretty good.

The people holding up the internet | Data Drop #

The reality is that so much of the software our world runs on was written by a really small number of people. This site does a great job of highlighting those folks and showing their accomplishments. These are the names we should respect versus the founders of social networks.

The nnxyz rooms #

Years ago I discovered the work of nnxyz on nifty.ink. I acquired a few of his pieces and grew to like it more and more. I ended up collecting four complete collections of hundreds of pieces. I had always wished to create a gallery like experience for anyone to experience. With the help of AI I was able to make that vision a reality.

Check out the nnxyz rooms.

Some highlights of what the website has.

  • Every drawing can be watched being made. The 574 Nifty Ink works are rebuilt from their archived brush strokes as native vector images, and each one replays stroke by stroke, with the recorded order, widths, colors and transparency.
  • Hung like a museum, not a feed. Six wings, 28 rooms, 626 works. Every work hangs in exactly one room, rooms hold 20 to 30 works, and each room is hung in the order the works were drawn, so a walk through a room is a walk through a few weeks of drawing.
  • Wall text in a museum voice. Each room has an introduction, chapters, labels, one-line notes, explained comparisons and a closing.
  • An audio tour in every room. Press play and a voice reads the room while each work comes on screen, about seven minutes a room, with pause, skip and a progress line.
  • A screen saver that draws. One work at a time, drawn stroke by stroke on black, held with its caption, then the next. Fullscreen, with your choice of drawing speed and hold time, and it can be limited to one room.
  • A map of the building. The collection as a three-floor museum map, rooms sized by how many works they hold, colored by collection, with doors between consecutive rooms and stairs between floors.
  • Readable by machines too. /llms.txt indexes the site for language models and /llms-full.txt carries the complete gallery text in one file.
  • Light or dark. A white gallery by default, black by choice, remembered across visits. The artwork itself is never altered.
  • Everything downloadable. Each artwork page offers the native SVG, the original PNG and the archived metadata and provenance records, with a link to the collected NFT.

I hope you like browsing and experiencing nnxyz’s work as much as I do. I feel like it has real movement and energy in it. nnxyz himself uses the term “thrash-art” — I dig it! I’ve never liked the VR gallery experiences online and I think this museum walk through, particularly with audio guidance, is a better way to experience it.

From Thingy, my agentic librarian

In past years, readers of The Weekly Thing have funded the Electronic Frontier Foundation and Creative Commons through Supporting Membership. This year the giving goes to Signal: free, open-source, end-to-end encrypted messaging that runs on donations rather than advertising, which is what keeps it independent. The newsletter itself is free and stays free. A year of Supporting Membership is $48, and 100% of it goes to Signal. You are welcome to join the readers giving this way.


Journal #

Saturday #

9:30 PM — We took Tammy’s Mom to her first MN United game! It looked like we might get to see a win and sing Wonderwall but alas, the Loons did not hold the lead.

Sunday #

4:11 PM — My Maker Space is now in a totally workable and ready spot!

Whitman on Walls! — Mazie, Tammy, and I went to the Parkway tonight for the Whitman on Walls show. We weren’t sure exactly what we were in for but it was a cool mashup of music, poetry, and video.

Minnesota poets respond to Walt Whitman’s iconic words in a “Poetry Slam and Jazz Improvisation Meets Film Screening” at The Parkway Theater. In honor of the 250th Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence and the iconic poet Walt Whitman’s celebration of the American people and their indestructible spirit, New York-based theatre collective Compagnia de’ Colombari’s film screening meets live performance event, Whitman on Walls!.

In collaboration with Minnesota Poets Collective, John Munson, and Steve Sutherland, sponsored by Calamus Project, and featuring a live music trio led by Dean Magraw (guitar), with Liz Draper (upright bass) and Suwal Singh (Tabla), will accompany the MN poets: Ashley Gray, Mishal Mazin, Suheb Rumi, Timothy Frantzich, Allen Wilcox, Erik Riese, and Christian Worby. Colombari created a series of seven short films featuring 50 actors performing Whitman’s “Song of Myself.”

Tuesday #

8:30 PM — Great time connecting with BigCharts alumni Steve Sutherland and Jim Rikkers!

9:00 PM — Cold and rainy weather put a damper on the evening but it was still cool to watch John Munson play with Steve Sutherland and I’m not remembering the guitar player’s name in a backyard show.

Wednesday #

10:00 PM — We saw Sting tonight at the Orpheum. It was really cool to see a music legend in such a small venue. It was a great show including a wide range of his catalog. According to Wikipedia he is 75 years old but doesn’t seem like it!

Thursday #

9:21 PM — I added a new Upcoming feature to Release Notes:

Release Notes now has a new section for what’s coming next. In Upcoming you can save birthdays, anniversaries, trips, and one-time events. You can choose when you would like these events to show up in your Release Notes. Trips include a destination with a start and end date. All of these upcoming events are private to only you.

Weekly Thing 353 · October 10, 2026

Release Notes for Every Day

Your Version Number Release Notes, Claude Haiku 5.5, zkAPI, hard budget caps, Tufte's Razor, M8 Ultra servers, Twin Cities Marathon.

Jamie Thingelstad
2,746 words · ~14 min read · 16:58 listen

✨ Explore with Thingy Download the MP3

Good morning! 👋

This week I felt like I was able to land a couple of projects that have long been on my list or I had recently picked up. It is really cool that agentic coding tools allow you to make the impossible list possible, but there is still only so many things you can push along at the same time.

Currently #

Building: I was thinking about Your Version Number and lightweight journaling. I think it would be fun to attach “release notes” to each day’s version. So I created Your Version Number: Release Notes. I’ve been using it for a couple of days and I really enjoy getting an email each day and simply replying to that email with notes from the day. It is easy, lightweight, and yet powerful since you can add photos and even send audio back. There is a full web interface and you can export all your data. If lightweight journaling is interesting to you give it a try. 📝

The gourds of fall! 🍂

Oct 9, 2026 · Minneapolis, MN

Notable #

Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 Anthropic #

I’ve been hoping to see a new version of Haiku for a long time and it is finally here. I moved a handful of projects to it the night it was released. With all the focus being on the most capable models, why care about Haiku?

When you are building agentic workloads you inevitably have various tasks that you need to deliver very cheaply and Haiku is the workhorse behind much of that. I probably run 100 times more Haiku calls compared to Sonnet and Opus. So the volume is there and you need this to work really well.

Additionally because Haiku was so old it didn’t have the effort and other modern capabilities of the newest models. That is now fixed so developers can rely on the same mechanics and work across various Claude models with ease. 👏

Also see Simon Willison’s post on Haiku 5.5.

We’re going to need default hard budget caps on pretty much everything #

I read this article with a smile as over the last few months I’ve added this as a feature to nearly every agentic workload that I run.

Here’s a product feature which the world is going to need a whole lot more of over the coming months and years: default hard budget caps. I’m talking about the feature of pay-by-usage services and APIs that lets you say “after $X/month, cut this thing off and return errors”. These need to be hard limits. Soft caps, “after $X/month, send me a warning email”, will not cut it.

By the way you can do this with the agentic loop having awareness. One of the agent projects I’ve been working on gets a hard monthly spend limit. From that limit it derives a budget and determines each day how it is pacing to that budget. So, not only can you make these systems cost-controlled but you can hand over part of the challenge of managing that to the system itself.

We definitely need this on the low end of the market for small and personal projects, however it is just as badly needed at the enterprise side. I can’t tell you how many vendors I’ve seen that move to credit models and they rather conveniently have no way to allow you to hard-cap the spend. This forces you as the customer to have to keep track or end up on the wrong side of a negotiation after you’ve burned through credits.

Introducing zkAPI: private usage credits for any API #

I’ve been suggesting that crypto is a better way for agents to handle payment for services for a bit. Here is a broader example of generally using crypto to pay for service usage without having to divulge your identity with it.

zkAPI separates payment from identity. You deposit credits (ETH, USDC, etc.) into a vault contract on Ethereum, one ordinary transaction. From then on, your balance exists as a private note: digital cash that only you can spend and that nobody can trace back to the deposit.

To authorize spending, software on your machine produces a small zero-knowledge proof that says, in effect, that a funded note covers this spend and nobody has spent it before. One proof can cover a single request or a whole session. The server can check that the statement is true without learning which note, which deposit, or which person. At the payment layer, requests do not link to you, and they do not link to each other.

I’m glad that folks are thinking about this. The speed of the web shouldn’t be limited by the pace of bank settlements and we shouldn’t have to forego our privacy in exchange for simply using an API.

On the Rumored M8 Ultra AI Servers #

I keep thinking about the strategic advantage that Apple finds itself in with the M-series chips and AI.

If an M8 Ultra server carries forward the unified-memory architecture and performance-per-watt advantages of Apple’s current chips, it could be an interesting machine for private AI inference. Its job would be narrower than replacing Nvidia across the industry. Instead, it gives buyers another credible option for private workloads that demand local control without wasting power.

It is unique that Apple can put enough compute power in a box that can sit on a desk, be powered with a regular outlet, not require special cooling, and be quiet enough to not need to be in a room of its own. For a number of professions and use cases with AI I also suggest we are going to want to go opposite of the last 20 years of cloud migration and run that workload locally. The most precise cost management we can have is running something on our own hardware. And if you are dealing with sensitive data running it locally is a great way to protect it.

Apple could be a big player in this space because of their unique advantage in compute power per watt.

Tufte’s Razor · An interactive guide to the data-ink ratio #

I’ve gone to Tufte’s data visualization seminars multiple times and always walk away with the general concept that some ways of visualizing numbers are just used to fill space. Have 5 numbers but need to fill a whole slide? Pie charts to the rescue.

This is a really well done interactive explorer that allows you to tweak things and see the impact.

The list of 11 checks for any visualization is a good review:

  1. The title says what the chart shows.
  2. Every number has its unit.
  3. Each value is said once.
  4. Nothing is shaded, boxed or outlined without a reason.
  5. Bars fill about half to two-thirds of their space.
  6. Bars start at zero.
  7. Labels sit next to what they name.
  8. Long names go on horizontal bars.
  9. Categories are sorted, unless they have an order of their own.
  10. The one thing that matters stands out.
  11. Every word is readable at arm’s length.

Help bring better charts to the world.

mb 2.0 with MCP support #

In March I created mb, a command-line micro.blog client that is specifically created for agents to use. This is what Otto uses to publish on its blog. It can also read the micro.blog timeline, follow people on micro.blog, and a variety of other features.

Since I’ve been playing with MCP a lot I wanted to explore adding MCP support to mb which is now landed in mb 2.0! In addition to MCP support I also created a Homebrew “tap” for it to make it super easy to install, added support for an mb --doctor command to help with setup, and a bunch more.

To try it the easiest thing is to use Homebrew:

Read the blog post for the full details.

From Thingy, my agentic librarian

This issue spent some time on privacy, from paying for services without handing over your identity to keeping sensitive work on your own hardware. Signal does that work for everyday conversation: end-to-end encrypted messaging and calling, an open source protocol, and no data collection. It is funded by donations, and in this ninth year of Supporting Membership it is where 100% of member fees go. A year of Supporting Membership is $48, and you are warmly invited to join in.


Journal #

Saturday #

11:30 AM — Today is that sad day when I take the boat in to be put in storage for the winter. Until next summer Magic Waves!

12:00 PM — My newest MCP experiment was to add it in WT Builder and then Claude was able to watch me creating content in near real-time through tool calls and give me immediate feedback on typos and grammar suggestions.

9:30 PM — We went to BRKTHROUGH tonight and tried out their various games. We’ve been to Activate many times. BRKTHROUGH seems like a good place for a larger group and adds food and beer options. We found Activate’s games better though.

Sunday #

7:02 AM — Working with Otto this morning to create a new version of my mb utility that will extend features and provide an MCP interface for agents to interact with micro.blog.

10:19 AM — Had a great time cheering on the Twin Cities Marathon runners this morning!

9:17 PM — I was inspired by the time analysis I had Claude do last week on what it took to send the Weekly Thing so I decided to build in some additional logging and a better visualization. Now I get a report like this for each issue I send. WT352 showed some benefits from my new automation! 🪄

Tuesday #

Weekly Thing Archive Improved — Over the 10 years that I’ve published the Weekly Thing I have used three different platforms to send it. Each one of those had unique requirements for how I structured the issues. For a while I’ve wanted to get the entire archive updated so that no matter how far you go back the issues have the similar structure that they have today. With the help of Claude I was able to make this happen! The full archive is now updated renders cleanly. It required pretty extensive source doctoring behind the scenes.

Along with that I was able to then render every issue in audio as well. Now the Weekly Thing Podcast feed goes all the way back to the very first issue as well which is pretty cool.

10:00 PM — We got to watch the US Men’s National Team take on Canada tonight in an international friendly. USMNT won 1-0. There was an impressive amount of fireworks to go with the game and the stands were completely full with long lines to get into Allianz Field. Great to see so much enthusiasm for soccer!

Wednesday #

6:11 PM — Thingy, my digital librarian, got a big improvement this week with a brand new design and moving its reasoning to the 5.5 level models (Sonnet for subscribers, Opus for supporting members). I’m very happy with how this is working now!

Briefly #

Article feels like click-bait but the three items it highlights are spot on. This is what I’ve been working to learn and adapt to first-hand with various projects I have. → AI is changing developer work. Here are three skills to strengthen.

These are all really important capabilities to have for any technology team. By the way, all of them need to also be enabled for agents. A Developer MCP is nearly a must-have way to connect this all together. → If You Understand These 5 Platform Engineering Terms, You’re Ahead of 90%

Interesting platform from Cloudflare all built on Git but I have to say their message here doesn’t seem focused enough on a specific solution. → We want you to build the next Git platform on Cloudflare

Things change so fast in AI that I don’t think you could ever rule in or out a specific solution. Also, I personally have found that MCP is a great way to force contextual thinking around tools. Sometimes command-lines represent the same thing, but not always. → “you said no mcp!” | earendil

It is worth keeping an eye on Pi. I suspect that we are going to see it embedded in a ton of different places that coding agents need to work in. → Pi 1.0 | Earendil

Good examples of using Jev inside of SQL statements. Jev is a “function call backed by frontier intelligence”. A lot of engineers I know are really excited about this because you can put it in very clear places in existing systems. → Jev and DuckDB: Plain-English Conditions in SQL

I use the OpenAI TTS models to create the audio versions of the Weekly Thing. I guess I’m lucky that the voices I use were not affected. → OpenAI silences familiar voices

This article had me thinking about the book Ishmael. When we left agricultural society and stopped growing our own food we have been on a continuous path of ever more interdependence. → The future of independence is interdependence

I don’t play with memecoins and this article is a good explainer on why nobody should. → The Death and Life of the Average Memecoin

Very few people manage their own domains for email. I do for multiple domains. It isn’t simple but it also isn’t that hard. This is a good overview if you ever want to move off of free email. Fastmail is what I use and they have a great step-by-step for this as well. → How to set up SPF, DKIM, and DMARC for your sending domain

Love seeing a new feed reader product land in the market. This looks really well done but I’ll stick with my Feedbin setup. If you are looking for a solution, give this a look. → Birchfeed

Reasonably good recommendations about any kind of blogging. → Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging · Refactoring English

This is such a fun little site. I love whole products that work in a URL. This has a lot of handy extensions like timers and QR codes. → BIGWORDS.PAGE: Turn any screen into a sign

I 💛 the Mandelbrot fractal. → Mandelnaut — Making Fractal Wallpapers

I suspect this weekend is going to be the warmest last days we have here in Minnesota. Time to get out and enjoy it!

Pumpkins on hay bales
